candidates.quote: In a bull trend, buy a 60 to 70 percent pullback from the current high, risking to a lower low, and taking profit at or above a new high (the reward is about twice the risk, the probability is about 60 percent).
candidates.description: In a bull trend, place a buy-limit order at a fixed retracement fraction of the current leg's high-to-low range (e.g. a Fibonacci-style 62 percent pullback), risking to a lower low and targeting a new high.
candidates.book_order_type: buy limit order at the fixed-percent retracement level

complexity.reason: needs swing-leg high/low tracking (a pivot-based measure) to compute the retracement level

notes: Merges this bullet with the book's later Fibonacci-62-percent discussion (page 195-196), the same idea at a slightly different named fraction (60-70% vs. 62%); one parameterized rule covers both.
Brooks explicitly prefers waiting for the bar to close bullish and buying a stop above its high over blindly buying this limit level; recorded as a caveat, not a separate candidate.

candidates.name: SecondEntryAddOnAtEntryBarLowLimitEntry
candidates.quote: if you just bought a second-entry setup in a pullback following a breakout above a bear trend line and a strong bull reversal bar, and the market tests the exact low of the entry bar a couple of times over the next one or two bars, consider placing a limit buy order to double your position at one tick above the low of the entry bar and risk just two ticks.
candidates.description: After a second-entry long following a bear-trend-line breakout and a strong bull reversal bar, if price re-tests the entry bar's exact low a couple of times over the next bar or two, place a buy-limit order one tick above the entry bar's low to double the position.
candidates.book_order_type: buy limit order one tick above the low of the entry bar, to double the position

complexity.reason: needs a persistent entry-bar-low reference and a retest counter across bars since entry

candidates.name: StopBeyondLineForFailedBreakoutAllowance
candidates.quote: traders who fade a test of the extremes by shorting at the resistance line above or buying at the support line below put their protective stops far enough beyond the line to allow for a failed breakout before the market reverses in their direction and tests the opposite side of the range.
candidates.description: When fading a test of a trend line, trend channel line, or trading-range extreme, place the protective stop far enough beyond that line/level to tolerate a small failed-breakout overshoot rather than sitting right at the line.
candidates.book_order_type: protective stop placed beyond the faded line by a fixed overshoot allowance

complexity.reason: the stop level itself is trivial arithmetic but depends on the trend-line/channel-line projection this exit is built on

candidates.name: FadeOppositeOfMismatchedCountingSetup
candidates.quote: In a bull channel, you should not be looking for low 1, 2, 3, or 4 setups, because those are setups only in bear trends and trading ranges. If you see one in a bull trend, since the odds are that it will fail and hit the protective buy stop above, it makes more sense to take the opposite trade. Instead of looking to short below the low of the prior bar, place a limit order to buy at or below that bar.
candidates.description: When a low1-4 short-counting setup forms inside a bull channel (a mismatched, against-trend counting setup, see R26-03), rather than skip it, trade the opposite side: place a buy-limit order at the same price level the mismatched short setup would have used as its trigger.
candidates.book_order_type: buy limit order at or below the mismatched short setup's trigger level

complexity.reason: reuses the H/L-N counting-setup primitives plus a channel-context classification

notes: Composes with ranges chapter 26's R26-03 (BarCountingSetupDirectionMustMatchTrend), reusing the same mismatch condition but acting on it (trade the opposite side) instead of just filtering.

candidates.name: ScaleInStopAndReverseOnSecondAdverseSignal
candidates.quote: There is one important caveat for traders who scale into countertrend trades, and that is that you should exit or reverse to the with-trend direction on the second move against you. This means that if you are scaling into shorts in a bull trend, exit or even reverse to long on a high 2, especially if it is near the moving average.
candidates.description: When scaling into a countertrend position, if a second with-trend counting setup (e.g. a high2 while short in a bull trend) fires against the position, especially near the moving average, exit the countertrend position or reverse to the with-trend direction, overriding the open countertrend position.
candidates.pseudocode:
isSecondAdverseWithTrendSignal = isHigh2SetupSignalBar[0] && isBullTrend[0]; // while short (countertrend) in a bull trend
allowExitOrReverseToLong = ctx.MarketPosition() == -1 && isSecondAdverseWithTrendSignal;
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (permission to exit/reverse an open countertrend position on the with-trend counting-setup entry)

complexity.reason: reuses the H2/L2 counting-setup primitives and a position-state read; the MA-proximity emphasis is a strengthening condition, not a hard requirement

notes: Reads position state to permit a reversal, in the style of the catalog's FlatOrOpenLossExceeds rule.

candidates.name: IiiPatternPrimitive

candidates.description: Shared primitive: an 'iii' pattern is three consecutive inside bars (each bar inside the range of the one before it).
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (bar-pattern classification used as a signal precondition)

complexity.reason: three chained inside-bar comparisons over fixed offsets

notes: Extends R28-05's ii pattern by one more inside bar; both patterns are traded the same way (a limit order a tick or two beyond the pattern's extreme) in this chapter's worked examples.

candidates.name: AvoidBlindSpikeFadeWithoutContext
candidates.quote: A strong spike alone is not a reason to begin to look to enter on a pullback using a limit order... A strong bull spike alone is not enough of a reason to buy a pullback on a limit order; traders need to consider the context of the bull spike.
candidates.description: Block limit-order countertrend pullback entries against a strong spike unless there is additional context beyond the spike itself (e.g. one of this chapter's other qualifying setups); a bare 'it spiked' observation is not sufficient.

// research: 'additional context' is intentionally left to the other named setups in this chapter/R26-01's reason list
allowSpikePullbackLimitFade = isStrongSpike[0] && hasAdditionalQualifyingContext[0];

complexity.reason: 'additional context' has no bar-level test of its own in this passage; it is a design decision to enumerate which sibling conditions qualify

rejected.quote: If you missed placing your stop entry order for the original entry by a few seconds and are trying to get in at the original price, place a limit order at the original price or a tick worse.

rejected.quote: Scale into any trade where you believe that your premise is strong.
rejected.reason: pure discretion, no bar-level test proposed

rejected.quote: A market order is just a type of limit order where a trader is eager to get in or out of a trade and does not worry about saving a tick or two.

chapter_summary: By far the largest source of new candidates in this batch: a long bulleted catalog (pages 192-194) of concrete limit-order entry setups, almost all sharing the same shape (a context/pattern classification gating a limit price placed at or near a bar extreme, moving average, trend line, or measured-move target), mechanized per this chapter's convention of deciding the condition on the completed bar and testing the following bar's high/low against the limit price. New shared primitives defined here: ii/iii inside-bar patterns (R28-05, R28-46, both composing the catalog's existing InsideBar rule), a measuring-gap primitive (R28-03), an always-in-flip primitive (R28-07, likely duplicating a trends-book primitive), a micro-channel primitive (R28-17, likely duplicating trends chapter 16), and a ledge primitive (R28-22). The worked examples in the back half of the chapter (Figures 28.1-28.5, pages 197-201) mostly re-illustrate these same setups plus already-mined patterns (wedge, dueling lines, expanding triangle, always-in, breakout tests) and did not yield further new candidates beyond a stop-placement rule for fading lines with an overshoot allowance (R28-43), a rule for trading the opposite side of a trend-mismatched counting setup (R28-44), a stop-and-reverse override for countertrend scale-ins (R28-45), an add-on entry at a re-tested entry-bar low (R28-42), and a filter against fading a spike on context alone (R28-47). Complexity skews hard/research throughout because nearly every setup is gated by a phase or pattern classification (spike vs. channel, early vs. late channel, always-in, trading-range day, stairs pattern) that this chapter assumes rather than defines.
